query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the ability of the X element (Si, Mn, or Al) to preferentially diffuse and oxidize at the surface governs the formation of a coherent, low‐stress protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C. This beneficial segregation promotes the formation of a continuous spinel or oxide phase with a close lattice match to the underlying alloy, which in turn minimizes stress and prevents cracking or spallation under oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in either a single-phase or multiphase solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative or corrosive environment (>900 °C) with controlled atmosphere composition; comparisons made between alloys with and without the favorable X element enrichment.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and continuity of a protective oxide scale (e.g., a coherent spinel and/or Al2O3/SiO2 rich layer) that is well lattice-matched with the alloy substrate.
generation.mechanism: The X element, due to its higher oxygen affinity and suitable diffusivity, segregates to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure and reacts to form a stable oxide. This oxide, by virtue of its crystallographic compatibility and low growth-induced stress, adheres coherently to the substrate. In multiphase alloys, uniform enrichment of X across phases is critical; otherwise, microstructural mismatches enhance local stress, leading to unstable, spalled oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with appropriate X content and homogeneous distribution will form a uniform, adherent, and stable oxide scale with reduced cracking or spallation compared to alloys lacking the beneficial X segregation. These alloys will exhibit lower oxide spallation rates and better protection against further oxidation and corrosive attack.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNi alloy variant without the X element addition or with insufficient X segregation, leading to the formation of less coherent, higher-stress oxide scales that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to high-entropy alloys in both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid-solution states when exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. It may not hold under significantly lower temperatures or in fundamentally different alloy systems where oxide growth dynamics differ markedly.
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxide phase (spinel vs. pure Al2O3 or SiO2) that forms and the quantitative improvement in spallation resistance depend on the nature and concentration of the X element and the microstructural distribution in multiphase alloys. Also, detailed kinetics of the X element segregation and resulting oxide scale formation remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one set with a controlled, sufficient level of the X element (Si, Mn, or Al) and one baseline set without it. Ensure both sets are processed to achieve similar single or multiphase solid-solution microstructures. Expose both sets to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed time. Post-exposure, characterize the oxide scale using techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology, and adhesion tests (e.g., scratch tests) to evaluate coating integrity. Additionally, measure weight change to assess oxidation kinetics.
measurements: Phase composition and structure of the oxide layer (via XRD)
Morphology and continuity of the oxide scale (via SEM)
Adhesion strength of the oxide layer (via scratch tests or similar)
Weight change as a metric of oxidation rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with sufficient X content do not exhibit a significantly more uniform, adherent, and stable oxide scale—with measurable reductions in spallation and oxidation rate—compared to the baseline alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
